summary: This unit gives you the everyday maths every trade needs: whole numbers and the order of operations, fractions, decimals and percentages, ratios for mixing, metric units and conversions, perimeter, area and volume, circles, money, time and averages, and simple formulas. You will learn to estimate before you calculate, to show your working, and to check every answer, so that you cut, mix, order and charge correctly.

blocks.p: This unit is shared by several Level 2 programmes at the Centre: welding, electrical installation, cosmetology and beauty therapy. Every one of these trades uses maths every day: a cutting list for a gate, the cable for a circuit, colour and developer for a client, a cleaning solution, the time a treatment ends, the price of a job, the paint for a wall or the water a tank will hold.

**Who it is for:** every trainee. You do not need to be "good at maths". You need to know which method to use, to set your working out neatly, and to check your answer. The worked examples come from several trades; the methods are the same in all of them.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Add, subtract, multiply and divide, and use the right order of operations (BODMAS).
Find fractions of amounts, change between fractions, decimals and percentages, and round sensibly.
Find a percentage of an amount, add tax or profit, take off a discount, add a waste allowance.
Mix products by ratio, and scale amounts and prices up or down.
Use metric units of length, mass, capacity and time, change between them, and measure accurately.
Work out perimeter, area and volume
Rectangles, triangles, circles and box shapes; the materials and paint for a job; what a tank holds.
Totals, change, unit prices, durations, 12-hour and 24-hour times, hours worked.
Find a mean, and put numbers into a formula such as V = I × R.
Estimate first, check by working backwards, and keep the units and the decimal point right.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of calculations and short questions on every topic in this kit.
A **written paper** with short answers (give the number **and** the unit) and longer answers where you must show every step of your working.

**Two group practicals.** In the first, you measure a real area at the Centre in millimetres, change the measurements to metres, work out the area, take away any door or window, and use the coverage and prices on a card to work out how many tins to buy, with 10% for waste, rounded up, and the total cost. In the second, you mix coloured water by ratio (for example 1 : 4, 1 : 9, 1 : 2), measure it in jugs read at eye level, label each mix, and work out the cost of each batch and the cost per 100 ml.

blocks.note: Write the unit with every answer (mm, m², ml, J$, hours). In the written paper, show each step: a correct method earns marks even if one figure slips.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Money in this kit is in Jamaican dollars (J$); exam papers may write just $. Large numbers are written with a space between groups of three digits (12 500; 1 250 000). You will also see commas used (12,500); they mean the same.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Whole numbers and the order of operations

head: Operation
Words that tell you to use it
Example
rows: Three cable runs of 14 m, 23 m and 9 m: 14 + 23 + 9 = 46 m
A 50 m roll after 46 m is used: 50 − 46 = 4 m left
6 frames, each needing 4 corner plates: 6 × 4 = 24 plates
share, split, each, per, how many in
A pack of 120 cotton rounds shared between 8 stations: 120 ÷ 8 = 15 each

blocks.p: When a calculation has more than one operation, they must be done in the right order, or the answer will be wrong. **BODMAS** gives the order:

head: Letter
Stands for
What to do
rows: Work out anything in brackets first
Next, working from left to right
Last, working from left to right

ul: 18 ÷ 3 × 2 = 6 × 2 = **12**: division and multiplication go from left to right (not 18 ÷ 6 = 3).

blocks.note: A scientific calculator follows BODMAS. A simple four-function calculator, and some phone calculators, may work from left to right as you press the keys. To be safe, work out brackets and multiplications first and write each result down.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1 000 moves the digits 1, 2 or 3 places to the left; dividing moves them to the right. 35 × 10 = 350; 2.4 × 1 000 = 2 400; 175 ÷ 100 = 1.75; 820 ÷ 1 000 = 0.82. You will use this all the time when you change units.

flow: Read the whole question
Write down what you know, with the units
Decide which operations you need
Estimate the answer
Work it out, one step to a line
Check the answer is sensible and answers the question, with its unit

blocks.p: A **fraction** is part of a whole. The bottom number (denominator) is how many equal parts the whole is split into; the top number (numerator) is how many of those parts you have. 3/4 means 3 of 4 equal parts.

ul: **Equivalent fractions** are equal: 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8 = 50/100.
**Simplify** by dividing the top and bottom by the same number: 12/16 = 3/4 (both divided by 4).
**Add or subtract** fractions with the same bottom number by adding or subtracting the tops: 3/8 + 1/8 = 4/8 = 1/2.
**A fraction of an amount:** divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top: 3/4 of 2 400 mm = 2 400 ÷ 4 × 3 = 1 800 mm.
**Multiply fractions:** top × top over bottom × bottom: 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2.
**Fraction to decimal:** divide the top by the bottom: 5/8 = 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625.
**Adding and subtracting:** line up the decimal points, and fill gaps with zeros: 15.6 + 2.45 → 15.60 + 2.45 = 18.05.

**Multiplying:** multiply as if there were no decimal points, then count the decimal places in the question and put the same number in the answer: 3.5 × 1.2 → 35 × 12 = 420 → two decimal places → 4.20 = 4.2.
**Dividing by a decimal:** multiply both numbers by 10 (or 100) until you are dividing by a whole number: 6 ÷ 0.4 = 60 ÷ 4 = 15. Check: 0.4 × 15 = 6.

blocks.p: Look at the digit just after the place you are rounding to. If it is 5 or more, round up; if it is 4 or less, leave the digit as it is.

ul: 4.36 to one decimal place → 4.4.
12.849 to two decimal places → 12.85.
3 742 to the nearest hundred → 3 700.
J$5 650 to the nearest J$100 → J$5 700.

blocks.note: When you buy material or tins of paint, round **up**, not to the nearest: 2.1 tins means you must buy 3 tins. When you count how many whole pieces you can cut from a bar, round **down**: 4.8 pieces means 4 full pieces.
blocks.label: Remember

head: To
Method
Example
rows: Find a percentage of an amount
Divide by 100 and multiply by the percentage, or multiply by the decimal
10% = divide by 10; 5% = half of 10%; 1% = divide by 100
Write one number as a percentage of another
Work it out and add it on, or multiply by 1 + the decimal
Work it out and take it off, or multiply by 1 − the decimal
Change a decimal to a percentage

blocks.p: Offcuts, saw cuts and mistakes mean you always need a little more material than the drawing shows. Example: a job needs 36 m of 25 mm square tube, and the shop adds 10% for waste: 36 × 1.10 = 39.6 m. The tube comes in 6 m lengths: 39.6 ÷ 6 = 6.6, so order **7 lengths** (42 m).
A client adds a 12% tip to a J$5 500 treatment: 0.12 × 5 500 = J$660.

blocks.note: General Consumption Tax (GCT) is added to many bills in Jamaica. Use the current rate shown by the business or on the receipt; the method is the same as adding any percentage.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Adding a percentage and then taking the same percentage off does not bring you back to the start. J$10 000 + 10% = J$11 000; J$11 000 − 10% = J$9 900, because the second 10% is worked out on a bigger amount.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **ratio** compares amounts in parts. 1 : 3 means 1 part of the first thing to 3 parts of the second. The order matters: "colour : developer" or "concentrate : water" tells you which is which. Simplify a ratio by dividing both sides by the same number: 15 : 25 = 3 : 5 (both divided by 5).

flow: Add the parts to find the total number of parts
Divide the amount you need by the total parts: this is the size of one part
Multiply one part by each number in the ratio
Check that the amounts add up to the total

blocks.p: **Worked example.** You need 600 ml of a cleaning solution mixed 1 : 5 (concentrate : water). Total parts = 1 + 5 = 6. One part = 600 ÷ 6 = 100 ml. Concentrate = 1 × 100 = **100 ml**; water = 5 × 100 = **500 ml**. Check: 100 + 500 = 600 ml.
When you know one amount, multiply instead. A colour is mixed 1 : 1.5 (colour : developer). For 60 ml of colour you need 60 × 1.5 = 90 ml of developer.

blocks.note: "1 to 4" (1 : 4) means 1 part concentrate in **5** parts of mix. So 1 litre of mix holds 1 000 ÷ 5 = 200 ml of concentrate, not 250 ml. Dividing by the second number instead of the total is the most common mixing mistake.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Always use the maker's ratio. Too strong a mix can burn skin or scalp, damage hair or surfaces, and give off harmful fumes; too weak a mix may not clean, disinfect or colour properly. Measure, never guess.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Stand the jug or measuring cylinder on a flat surface.
Bend down so that your eye is level with the mark, and read at the bottom of the curved surface of the liquid.
Use a measuring cylinder or a syringe for small amounts.
Label every mix with what it is, the ratio and the date.

blocks.p: In **direct proportion**, when one amount goes up, the other goes up at the same rate. Find the value of **one** first (the unitary method). Example: 4 m of cable costs J$1 080. 1 m costs J$1 080 ÷ 4 = J$270, so 7 m cost 7 × J$270 = **J$1 890**.

In **inverse proportion**, when one amount goes up, the other goes down: more workers sharing a job take less time, as long as they all work at the same rate and do not get in each other's way. Example: 3 cleaners take 4 hours to clean a villa. That is 3 × 4 = 12 hours of work, so 2 cleaners take 12 ÷ 2 = **6 hours**.

A drawing at a scale of 1 : 20 means 1 mm on the paper stands for 20 mm on the real job. A line 35 mm long on the drawing is 35 × 20 = 700 mm on the job. Use the dimensions written on a drawing wherever they are given; measure off the paper only if you are told to.

head: Quantity
Units
Conversions
rows: 1 cm³ = 1 ml; 1 000 cm³ = 1 L; 1 m³ = 1 000 L

blocks.p: **To change to a smaller unit, multiply. To change to a bigger unit, divide.**

ul: 3.65 m to millimetres: × 1 000 = 3 650 mm.
820 mm to metres: ÷ 1 000 = 0.82 m.
64 cm to millimetres: × 10 = 640 mm.
2.75 m to centimetres: × 100 = 275 cm; 85 cm to metres: ÷ 100 = 0.85 m.
2 250 g to kilograms: ÷ 1 000 = 2.25 kg.
0.75 L to millilitres: × 1 000 = 750 ml.

blocks.note: Put every measurement into the same unit **before** you add, multiply or compare. 1.2 m + 350 mm = 1 200 mm + 350 mm = 1 550 mm, not 351.2.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Jamaica uses metric units, but you will still meet inches and feet: pipe and conduit sizes, some bolts and drill bits, plywood sheets of 4 ft × 8 ft, and steel lengths sold as 20 ft.

ul: 1 inch = 25.4 mm; 1/2 inch = 12.7 mm.
1 foot = 12 inches = 304.8 mm (about 305 mm).

blocks.h: Reading a metric tape or rule

ul: The smallest marks are millimetres; the numbered marks are usually centimetres (10 mm apart), often with a longer mark halfway at 5 mm.
Many tapes also show whole metres in red or bold: 1 m, 2 m, and so on.
Read the last numbered mark, then count the millimetres after it: 3 marks past 47 cm is 473 mm.
On a long tape, read the metre mark too: 1 m and 47.3 cm is 1 473 mm, or 1.473 m.
Use the right tool: a tape for long lengths, a steel rule for short ones, a caliper for small, exact sizes.
Hook the tape squarely on the end of the work, and keep it straight and flat.
Read the scale straight on, with your eye level with the mark.
Write the measurement down at once, with its unit.
Measure twice, cut once; ask someone to read the tape back to you.
Do not let a steel tape snap back: its edge can cut.

blocks.p: The **perimeter** is the distance all the way round the outside of a shape. For a rectangle, perimeter = 2 × (length + width). A frame 1.5 m by 0.9 m needs 2 × (1.5 + 0.9) = 2 × 2.4 = **4.8 m** of bar round the outside.

**Area** is the amount of flat surface, measured in square units such as m². You need it to work out how much sheet metal, paint, floor tiles, wall covering or cleaning product a job needs, and so what the materials will cost.

head: Shape
Formula
Example
rows: A gable end with a base of 5 m and a height of 1.8 m: 0.5 × 5 × 1.8 = 4.5 m²
π × r × r (πr²), with π about 3.14
A round table top 0.8 m across: r = 0.4 m; 3.14 × 0.4 × 0.4 = 0.50 m²

blocks.note: Change millimetres to metres **before** you multiply: 600 mm × 400 mm = 0.6 m × 0.4 m = 0.24 m². If you multiply first you get 240 000 mm², which you must divide by 1 000 000 (not 1 000) to get m².
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Measure: the wall is 4 200 mm long and 2 700 mm high, with a door 900 mm × 2 100 mm
Change to metres: wall 4.2 m × 2.7 m; door 0.9 m × 2.1 m
Wall area: 4.2 × 2.7 = 11.34 m²
Door area: 0.9 × 2.1 = 1.89 m²; take it away: 11.34 − 1.89 = 9.45 m²
Two coats: 9.45 × 2 = 18.9 m²
The tin says 1 litre covers 10 m²: 18.9 ÷ 10 = 1.89 litres
Add 10% for waste: 1.89 × 1.1 = 2.08 litres
Paint comes in 1-litre tins: round up to 3 tins; at J$2 350 a tin, 3 × 2 350 = J$7 050

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The middle point of the circle
A straight line from the centre to the edge
A straight line across the circle through the centre; d = 2 × r
The distance all the way round: C = π × d
A number a little more than 3: about 3.14 (3.142)

blocks.p: Example: a steel band is to go round a round tank 1.2 m across. C = 3.14 × 1.2 = 3.77 m, plus an allowance for the overlap or joint. When you roll a ring from flat bar, use the diameter measured to the middle of the bar's thickness.
**Volume** is the space inside a solid, measured in cubic units such as m³. For a box shape, volume = length × width × height (or depth). One cubic metre holds **1 000 litres**.

ul: A rectangular tank 1.6 m × 1.0 m × 0.75 m: 1.6 × 1.0 × 0.75 = 1.2 m³ = 1 200 litres.
In centimetres, change to metres first: 120 cm × 90 cm × 60 cm = 1.2 m × 0.9 m × 0.6 m = 0.648 m³ = 648 litres.
A round (cylinder) tank: volume = π × r × r × height. A tank 1.0 m across and 1.5 m high: r = 0.5 m; 3.14 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 1.5 = 1.18 m³, about 1 180 litres.

blocks.h: Working out materials for a job

flow: Read the drawing and list every part, with its size and how many
Change every size to the same unit
Work out the length, area or amount for each part, and add them up
Add an allowance for waste, often about 10%
Round up to the sizes you can buy, and check that the pieces will fit in those sizes

blocks.p: **Worked example: a tank stand.** 4 legs of 1 200 mm and 8 rails of 900 mm in angle iron. Legs: 4 × 1.2 = 4.8 m. Rails: 8 × 0.9 = 7.2 m. Total: 12.0 m. With 10% for waste: 12.0 × 1.1 = 13.2 m. The angle is sold in 6 m lengths: 13.2 ÷ 6 = 2.2, so order **3 lengths**. Check the pieces fit: one length gives 4 legs and 1 rail (5.7 m); a second gives 6 rails (5.4 m); the third gives the last rail and spare.

ul: **Totals from a price list:** 4 tubes of gel at J$1 850 and 2 files at J$420: 4 × 1 850 = 7 400; 2 × 420 = 840; total J$8 240.
**Change:** count up from the price to the amount paid. A bill of J$2 760 paid with J$5 000: J$2 760 + J$40 = J$2 800; + J$200 = J$3 000; + J$2 000 = J$5 000. Change = 40 + 200 + 2 000 = **J$2 240**.

**Unit price (best buy):** 500 ml for J$1 200 is J$1 200 ÷ 500 = J$2.40 per ml; 1 litre for J$2 100 is J$2 100 ÷ 1 000 = J$2.10 per ml. The litre is better value, if you will use it before it goes off.
**Cost of part of a pack:** concentrate at J$3 600 a litre costs J$3 600 ÷ 1 000 = J$3.60 per ml, so 150 ml costs 150 × J$3.60 = J$540.

**Cost of a mixed batch:** a 500 ml batch mixed 1 : 4 holds 500 ÷ 5 = 100 ml of concentrate. At J$2 800 a litre (J$2.80 per ml) that is 100 × J$2.80 = J$280. The batch is five lots of 100 ml, so the cost per 100 ml of mix is J$280 ÷ 5 = J$56.
**Foreign currency:** multiply by the rate. At J$155 to US$1, US$40 = 40 × 155 = J$6 200.
**Adding a duration:** start 13:50, job takes 2 hours 35 minutes. 13:50 + 2 h = 15:50; + 10 min = 16:00; + 25 min = **16:25**.
**Hours worked:** 08:15 to 17:00 is 8 hours 45 minutes; less a 45-minute lunch = **8 hours**.
**Minutes to hours:** 135 minutes = 2 hours 15 minutes = 2.25 hours.

**Several jobs in a row:** treatments of 1 h 15 min and 45 min, a 15-minute break, then a treatment of 1 h 30 min, starting at 09:30. 09:30 + 1 h 15 min = 10:45; + 45 min = 11:30; + 15 min = 11:45; + 1 h 30 min = **13:15**. Check: 75 + 45 + 15 + 90 = 225 minutes = 3 h 45 min, and 09:30 + 3 h 45 min = 13:15.

blocks.note: There are 60 minutes in an hour, not 100. On a calculator, 1.3 hours is 1 hour 18 minutes (0.3 × 60), not 1 hour 30 minutes.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The **mean** (the usual average) = the total ÷ the number of items. Example: five treatments took 45, 50, 40, 55 and 60 minutes. Total = 250 minutes; mean = 250 ÷ 5 = **50 minutes**. Use the mean to plan bookings, or to see how close a batch of cut parts is to its size.

The **range** (largest − smallest) shows how spread out the numbers are: 60 − 40 = 20 minutes. Do not confuse the mean with the most common value, or with the number halfway between the largest and the smallest.
A **formula** is a rule written with letters. Put the numbers in place of the letters (substitute), then work it out using BODMAS. Write the unit with the answer.

head: Formula
What the letters mean
Example
rows: V = voltage in volts (V); I = current in amps (A); R = resistance in ohms (Ω)
The same rule, arranged to find the current
The same rule, arranged to find the resistance
The power rule, arranged to find the current

blocks.note: Jamaica's mains supply is 110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz. Some books use 230 V or 240 V; the method is the same, but use the voltage of the supply you are actually working on.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Before you use a calculator, round each number to an easy value and work out a rough answer in your head. If the calculator's answer is far from your estimate, you have pressed a wrong key or put the decimal point in the wrong place.
Estimating also helps when there is no calculator, for example when a customer asks for a rough price on the spot.

ul: **Estimate first** and compare.
**Work backwards** with the opposite operation: if 7 × 4 980 = 34 860, then 34 860 ÷ 7 should give 4 980. For change, the price + the change should equal the amount paid.
**Do it again a different way**, for example 15% as 10% + 5%.
**Check the units and the decimal point.** Is 12.5 m a sensible width for a door? Is 1.25 m?
**Ask a co-worker** to check important figures.
**Re-measure** before you cut or mix.

blocks.note: Mistakes cost: a part cut short is scrap, a wrong mix can burn a client's scalp or damage a surface, and a wrong price loses money or customers.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise more examples.

ul: I can add, subtract, multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals, and use BODMAS.
I can find a fraction of an amount, simplify fractions, and change between fractions, decimals and percentages.
I can round to a given number of decimal places, and know when to round up or down at work.
I can find a percentage of an amount, add tax, a mark-up or a waste allowance, and take off a discount.
I can use a ratio to work out the amounts in a mix, and measure liquids accurately.
I can solve direct and inverse proportion problems, and use a scale drawing.
I can change between mm, cm, m and km; g and kg; ml and L; seconds, minutes and hours; and inches and millimetres.
I can find the perimeter of a rectangle and the area of rectangles, triangles and circles.
I can find the circumference of a circle and use the radius and the diameter correctly.
I can find the volume of a box-shaped or round tank and change cubic metres into litres.
I can work out the materials for a job, with a waste allowance, rounded up to the sizes I can buy.
I can work out totals, change, unit prices and currency conversions.
I can use the 12-hour and 24-hour clock, add times and work out hours worked.
I can find a mean and a range.
I can put numbers into a formula such as V = I × R or P = V × I.
I can estimate an answer and check a calculation in more than one way.

head: Mistake
Instead
rows: Change to one unit first: 1 200 + 350 = 1 550 mm
Dividing by the second number of a ratio (1 : 4 → ÷ 4)
Using the diameter in π × r × r
Halve the diameter to get the radius first
Rounding 6.2 lengths of tube down to 6
Giving an answer with no unit
Always write mm, m², L, J$ or hours

terms: The amount of flat surface, in square units such as m²
The order of operations: brackets, orders, division and multiplication, addition and subtraction
The distance round a circle: π × diameter
A digit after the decimal point
The bottom number of a fraction
A straight line across a circle through its centre; twice the radius
When one amount goes up, the other goes up at the same rate
A rough answer found by rounding, used to check a calculation
A rule written with letters, such as V = I × R
When one amount goes up, the other goes down, such as more workers and less time
The total divided by the number of items; the usual average
The top number of a fraction
The distance all the way round the outside of a shape
The number used for circles, about 3.14
A straight line from the centre of a circle to its edge
The largest value minus the smallest
A comparison of amounts in parts, such as 1 : 4
Making a number simpler to a given place, up or down
On a drawing, how the drawn size relates to the real size, such as 1 : 20
The cost of one unit, such as one ml, one metre or one item
The space inside a solid, in cubic units such as m³; 1 m³ = 1 000 L
Extra material added for offcuts and mistakes, often about 10%

c1.title: Gate frames in Bog Walk
c1.text: Tajay, a welder in Bog Walk, St Catherine, is making 3 identical gate frames from 40 mm square tube. Each frame is 1 800 mm wide and 1 500 mm high round the outside, with 4 inside bars of 1 420 mm each. The tube is sold in 6 m lengths at J$5 450 a length, and the shop adds 10% for offcuts and mistakes.

c2.title: Mixing at a salon in Lucea
c2.text: Lisa-Gaye works at a salon in Lucea, Hanover. A permanent colour is mixed with developer at 1 : 1.5 (colour : developer). The salon's surface cleaner is diluted 1 : 4 (concentrate : water), and the concentrate costs J$3 200 a litre. A full colour service takes 2 hours 20 minutes, and the salon closes at 18:00.

c3.title: Wiring a shop in Port Maria
c3.text: Akeem, an electrician in Port Maria, St Mary, is wiring a small shop from a drawing at a scale of 1 : 50, on which the main wall measures 128 mm. The shop's water heater draws 15 A from the 220 V supply, and a drinks cooler draws 6.5 A from the same supply. The hardware store offers him 12% off his materials bill of J$46 500.

c4.title: A tank and its base in Santa Cruz
c4.text: Mr Hylton in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth, is having a round plastic water tank set on a new concrete base. The tank is 1.5 m across and 1.8 m high. The base is 2.0 m × 2.0 m and 150 mm thick. A welder will make a steel guard rail to go once round the tank.

c5.title: A Saturday at a spa in Treasure Beach
c5.text: Annakay manages bookings at a small spa in Treasure Beach, St Elizabeth. On Saturday the spa gave six massages lasting 60, 75, 45, 90, 60 and 60 minutes. A massage costs J$6 800; one guest paid for hers with a US$50 note when the spa's rate was J$155 to US$1. A therapist worked from 08:45 to 17:15 with a 45-minute lunch.

questions.q: How much tube does one complete frame need, before any waste allowance?
questions.why: Outside: 2 × (1.8 + 1.5) = 6.6 m. Inside bars: 4 × 1.42 = 5.68 m. One frame: 6.6 + 5.68 = 12.28 m. Change 1 420 mm to 1.42 m before adding.

questions.q: How many 6 m lengths should Tajay order for all three frames, including the 10% allowance?
questions.why: Three frames: 3 × 12.28 = 36.84 m. With 10%: 36.84 × 1.1 = 40.52 m. 40.52 ÷ 6 = 6.75, which must be rounded up to 7 lengths: 6 lengths (36 m) would leave him short.

questions.q: What will Tajay's tube cost?
questions.why: He pays for whole lengths: 7 × J$5 450 = J$38 150. Check by estimating: 7 × J$5 500 = J$38 500, which is close.

questions.q: How many 1 420 mm inside bars can Tajay cut from one 6 m length?
o: 4 bars, with about 320 mm left over
4 bars, with about 580 mm left over
3 bars, with about 1 740 mm left over
questions.why: 6 000 ÷ 1 420 = 4.2, and you cannot use part of a bar, so round down to 4. 4 × 1 420 = 5 680 mm, leaving 6 000 − 5 680 = 320 mm (a little less after the saw cuts).

questions.q: Lisa-Gaye needs 150 ml of mixed colour in total for a client with long hair. How much colour and developer should she use?
questions.why: Total parts: 1 + 1.5 = 2.5. One part: 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 ml. Colour: 1 × 60 = 60 ml; developer: 1.5 × 60 = 90 ml. Check: 60 + 90 = 150 ml.

questions.q: How much concentrate goes into a 750 ml spray bottle of the surface cleaner?
questions.why: 1 : 4 means 1 part concentrate in 5 parts of mix. 750 ÷ 5 = 150 ml of concentrate, and 4 × 150 = 600 ml of water. Dividing by 4 instead of 5 gives the common wrong answer, 187.5 ml.

questions.q: What does the concentrate in one 750 ml bottle cost?
What is the latest time Lisa-Gaye can start a full colour service so that it ends by closing time?
questions.why: Count back from 18:00: 2 hours earlier is 16:00, and 20 minutes before that is 15:40, which is 3:40 p.m. Times are not decimals: 6.00 − 2.20 on a calculator gives 3.80, which leads to the wrong answer of 4:20.

questions.q: How long is the shop's main wall?
questions.why: At 1 : 50, every 1 mm on the drawing is 50 mm on site: 128 × 50 = 6 400 mm = 6.4 m. Check that it is sensible: a small shop wall of 64 m or 0.64 m is not.

questions.q: Using P = V × I, what is the power of the drinks cooler?
questions.why: P = V × I = 220 × 6.5 = 1 430 W. Estimate: 220 × 6 = 1 320, a little less, so the answer is about right.

questions.q: Using R = V ÷ I, what is the resistance of the water heater?
questions.why: R = V ÷ I = 220 ÷ 15 = 14.67, about 14.7 Ω. Multiplying the numbers (3 300) gives the heater's power in watts, not its resistance, and dividing the wrong way round gives 0.07.

questions.q: What is Akeem's materials bill after the 12% discount?
What volume of concrete is needed for the base?
questions.why: Change 150 mm to 0.15 m first. Volume = 2.0 × 2.0 × 0.15 = 0.6 m³. Using 150 without changing it gives 600 m³, far more than a small base could need.

questions.q: About how many litres will the tank hold when full?
questions.why: Radius = 1.5 ÷ 2 = 0.75 m. Volume = π × r × r × h = 3.14 × 0.75 × 0.75 × 1.8 = 3.18 m³, and 1 m³ = 1 000 L, so about 3 180 L. Using the diameter instead of the radius gives four times too much.

questions.q: What length of flat bar will the guard rail need, before any allowance for the joint?
questions.why: The distance round a circle is π × d = 3.14 × 1.5 = 4.71 m. π × r gives only half the way round, and π × r × r (1.77) is the area of the top, not a length.

questions.q: What was the mean (average) length of Saturday's massages?
questions.why: Add all six: 60 + 75 + 45 + 90 + 60 + 60 = 390 minutes. Divide by the number of massages, 6: 390 ÷ 6 = 65 minutes. 60 is only the most common time, and 78 comes from dividing by 5 instead of 6.

questions.q: How much change, in Jamaican dollars, should the guest get from her US$50 note?
questions.why: First change the currency: US$50 × 155 = J$7 750. Then take away the price: J$7 750 − J$6 800 = J$950. Check: J$6 800 + J$950 = J$7 750.

questions.q: How many hours did the therapist work, written as a decimal for her time sheet?
questions.why: 08:45 to 17:15 is 8 hours 30 minutes; less 45 minutes for lunch leaves 7 hours 45 minutes. 45 minutes is 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75 of an hour, so 7.75 hours. Writing 7.45 mixes up minutes and decimals.

questions.q: A trainee is checking a formula on a job sheet. What is the value of 36 − 12 ÷ 4 + 2?
questions.why: Division comes before addition and subtraction: 12 ÷ 4 = 3. Then work from left to right: 36 − 3 = 33, and 33 + 2 = 35.

questions.q: A 2 kg tub of wax at a beauty salon is three-fifths used. How many grams are left?
questions.why: If 3/5 is used, 2/5 is left. 2 kg = 2 000 g, so 2 000 ÷ 5 × 2 = 800 g. 1 200 g is the amount used, not the amount left.
